mcqs.question: Why doesn't a typical OLTP point lookup benefit from MPP the way a warehouse aggregation does?
options: OLTP databases are technically incapable of running on more than one machine
A point lookup targets a single row, so there's no large scan to split across nodes — parallelizing it adds coordination overhead without reducing the actual work
MPP only works with columnar storage, and OLTP databases never use columnar storage
Point lookups are always slower than aggregations regardless of architecture
mcqs.explanation: MPP pays off by splitting a large scan across many nodes; a point lookup that only touches one row has nothing substantial to split, so spreading it across a cluster only adds coordination cost. OLTP databases can run distributed, MPP doesn't strictly require columnar storage, and the relative speed depends on the query type, not a universal ranking.

mcqs.question: A table has 50 columns. A query runs `SELECT SUM(revenue) FROM sales`. Why does columnar storage make this faster than row storage?
options: Columnar storage only reads the revenue column's bytes, while row storage would have to read every column of every row to reach it
Columnar storage automatically caches the entire table in memory
Row storage cannot compute SUM aggregations at all
Columnar storage always stores less total data than row storage regardless of the query
mcqs.explanation: Since columnar layout groups each column's values together on disk, a query touching one column reads only that column's bytes; row layout would read every column of every row just to extract the one needed. Row storage can compute SUM fine, and the storage-size advantage, if any, is separate from this per-query read-efficiency benefit.

mcqs.question: What does separating storage and compute in a modern cloud warehouse make possible that a bundled architecture doesn't?
options: Running multiple independently-sized compute clusters against the same underlying data simultaneously, without duplicating it
Eliminating all network latency between storage and compute
Guaranteeing lower cost than a bundled architecture in every case
Removing the need for any compute cluster at all
mcqs.explanation: Decoupling lets independent compute clusters attach to the same stored data, so different teams' workloads don't compete for the same fixed resources — the core benefit of separation. It doesn't eliminate the storage-compute network hop, doesn't guarantee lower cost for every workload, and compute clusters are still required to actually run queries.

mcqs.question: Why can an unnecessarily broad query directly inflate a warehouse bill in a way it wouldn't on a fixed-price OLTP instance?
options: Warehouse pricing is unrelated to how much data a query scans
Most consumption-based warehouse pricing charges proportional to bytes scanned or compute time used, so a broader scan directly costs more
OLTP instances charge more per query than warehouses do
Warehouses only charge a flat monthly fee regardless of usage
mcqs.explanation: Because many warehouse pricing models bill by bytes scanned or compute-seconds, a query that scans more data than necessary directly increases cost — a mechanism a fixed-price OLTP instance simply doesn't have. Warehouse pricing is very much tied to scan volume, and flat monthly billing is the opposite of the usage-based model being described here.

mcqs.question: A team runs 'show this one customer's latest order' directly against the warehouse and finds it slower than expected. What's the correct fix?
options: Add more compute nodes to the warehouse cluster to speed up the lookup
Increase the warehouse's columnar compression settings
Move that specific point-lookup workload to an OLTP database or cache sized for single-row access patterns
Nothing — this latency is unavoidable for any data system
mcqs.explanation: Point lookups need an access pattern the warehouse isn't built for — the fix is architectural, moving that workload to a system designed for fast single-row access. More nodes or better compression address scan-heavy workloads, not single-row latency, and this latency is very much avoidable with the right system for the job.
